title: 'Passportmaxxing': H-1B Uncertainty Pushes Indians in US Toward Second Residencies
excerpt: A Dubai-based citizenship advisory firm says it has processed 450+ Indian clients for second passports as green-card backlogs and tougher visa enforcement turn mobility into an asset class.
body:
• Jeremy Savory, founder of Dubai-based citizenship advisory firm Savory & Partners, says Indian professionals in the US are increasingly buying second residencies and citizenships as a "Plan B" against H-1B and green-card uncertainty — a trend he calls "passportmaxxing."
  • His firm has processed more than 450 Indian clients for second passports and over 150 for residencies such as golden visas.
  • Savory cautions that India does not allow dual citizenship: for Indian passport holders, residency is "often the smarter first move."
  • The shift mirrors a broader mindset change among H-1B workers — from planning a life in America to planning for legal survival, as green-card queues stretch into decades.

Long green-card backlogs, tighter visa scrutiny and growing global uncertainty are pushing some Indian professionals and wealthy families in the United States to buy what amounts to an insurance policy on their mobility: a second residency or citizenship. Jeremy Savory, founder of Dubai-based Savory & Partners — one of the world's largest citizenship- and residency-by-investment advisory firms — calls the trend "passportmaxxing," and told The American Bazaar that the Indian community is now one of its fastest-growing client bases.

Having the choice

Savory describes global mobility as a modern asset class: a second residency, assets in more than one country, and a Plan B ready before it is needed. His framework runs through seven levels, from being "Exposed" under a single nationality, through education and eligibility, to a first second citizenship, real mobility, "jurisdiction stacks" covering tax, banking, schooling and estate planning, and finally a multigenerational family office spanning several jurisdictions. "It isn't about leaving," Savory said. "It's about having the choice." His firm has helped more than 12,000 clients secure second residencies and citizenships, including over 450 Indian clients for second passports and more than 150 for residencies.

"Many Indians in America have spent years, sometimes a decade, with their future sitting in another government's visa queue. That is exactly the loss of control that drives people to build a Plan B."

— Jeremy Savory, founder, Savory & Partners

Context & background

The demand has a clear policy backdrop. For September 2026, the US State Department lists India's EB-2 employment category as unavailable for final action, with EB-3 final action dates stuck at January 1, 2014 and EB-1 at October 15, 2022 — and all available FY2026 EB-2 immigrant visas for India already used. The per-country cap of 7% of the combined family and employment preference limits keeps Indian applicants in decades-long queues despite advanced degrees, high-paying jobs and years of US tax history. On the temporary side, the September 2025 rollback of the "dropbox" interview-waiver program forced most H-1B, L-1 and F-1 renewals back into in-person consular interviews, and enforcement has tightened. A study of the professional platform Blind, cited by The American Bazaar, found H-1B workers' searches shifting from Roth IRAs, 401(k)s and home purchases — which fell from 13.5 to 2.5 mentions per 1,000 H-1B searches — to layoffs, visa appointments and being "stuck" abroad. "The data suggests a shift from planning for life in the United States to planning for legal survival in the United States," the analysis noted.

"One thing that the Indian community needs to understand is that India doesn't allow dual citizenship. For anyone still holding an Indian passport, residency is often the smarter first move."

— Jeremy Savory, founder, Millionaire Migrant

Impact & analysis

What changed, Savory argues, is confidence. A decade ago, his clients were largely Middle Eastern families buying safety; today they are entrepreneurs and investors who object less to paying tax than to having no say over decisions that affect everything they have built. Countries now compete for individuals the way they once competed for factories, designing residency, citizenship and tax programs to attract mobile capital and talent. Savory expects Indian families to be "one of the defining stories of wealth mobility over the next decade," noting that India — neutral in the US-China rivalry — is keeping both the people and the money. Notably, the Plan B is not purely an exit story: many clients keep their base in India or the US and build optionality around it, a residency in Europe, a company in Dubai, property across two or three markets.

Diaspora angle

This is the diaspora story in its purest form: a community whose American dream was built on employer-sponsored visas is now pricing the risk of that dependence. For H-1B families, the practical takeaway from Savory's interview is narrower than the sales pitch — understand the dual-citizenship bar first, and weigh residency options that do not require surrendering an Indian passport.

What's next

Watch the monthly visa bulletins for movement in India's EB-2 and EB-3 dates, and the direction of H-1B policy through FY2026. Several European golden-visa programs are tightening or closing — timing matters for anyone considering the residency route.
